title: Vaishnava theology (Ramanuja's Sri Bhashya, selections)
hook: "I slept well": a sentence everyone says at breakfast becomes evidence in Ramanuja's argument about what awareness is

segments.voice: Yesterday in Vaishnava theology, knowing God became a thread of oil: steady remembrance, so vivid it's like seeing. What did you give one unbroken thread of attention? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-nine.
screen: `A THREAD OF OIL.` · `TODAY: THE LAMP AND ITS LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Breakfast. Someone asks how you slept, and you say, I slept well. Simple. But stop on it for a second. While you were in deep sleep, you weren't thinking, weren't dreaming, weren't aware of the room. So who slept well? And how does that someone know? Ramanuja uses exactly this ordinary sentence in the Sri Bhashya. It's part of a long argument about what consciousness is, and whether there's a someone inside it. The breakfast table, it turns out, is a good place to do theology. Today: the lamp and its light.
screen: `I SLEPT WELL.` → `WHO SLEPT, AND WHO KNOWS?` → `THE LAMP AND ITS LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Advaita teachers, in Shankara's line, say the deepest reality is pure consciousness, with no owner and no object, and that the sense of I is laid over it, like a snake seen on a rope. Ramanuja sets that view out at length, and then answers it. Every awareness we ever have, he says, has two features. It belongs to someone, and it shows something. I know the cup. I see the light. Awareness with no knower and nothing known isn't anything we've met. Then the breakfast line. When we wake and say I slept well, he argues, the I was there all along; it simply wasn't knowing much. So the self is a real knower, not a mask over knowing. To hold both, he uses a lamp. A lamp is bright in itself, and it also has light that spreads out from it into the room. The light is real, and it's the lamp's. In the same way, he says, the self is conscious by nature, and it has consciousness that reaches out toward things. In bondage that reach is narrowed, like light behind a shutter. In freedom it opens wide. Advaita teachers answer him in turn, and both schools keep reading. For Ramanuja, the point is this: there's a someone in your awareness, and that someone is real enough to love and to be loved.
screen: `AWARENESS BELONGS TO SOMEONE.` · `AND IT SHOWS SOMETHING.` · `THE LAMP AND ITS LIGHT.` · `NARROWED, THEN OPENED WIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice the lamp and its light. Sit, and let the breath settle. Let your attention rest on one sound in the room. Notice that there's a sound, and notice that it's being heard. Then let attention widen, the way light spreads, to every sound you can hear at once. Then narrow it again to one. Widen, narrow. Through all of it, notice the one who is noticing. If you pray, you can rest that noticing in the name you pray to. The bell holds the time.
Vaishnava theology. Today, Ramanuja's lamp: a self that is conscious by nature, with a light of awareness that narrows and opens wide. Today's word.

Your line: Vaishnava theology (Ramanuja's Sri Bhashya, selections). Today, when your attention narrows to one worry, notice it, and let the light open a little wider. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Sri Vaishnava students meet this argument in the Sri Bhashya's long opening section, studied with a teacher, where Ramanuja sets out the Advaita view in full and answers it; Advaita students study the replies made from their side.

fork.setup: you wake up and say, I slept well. you're Ramanuja. what does that sentence show you?
options: that the I was there through deep sleep.
that nobody was there at all.
fork.reveal: Ramanuja argues the I persists through deep sleep: a real knower that simply wasn't knowing much.

original.note: Sanskrit: attributive consciousness, the self's light of awareness in Ramanuja's school.

trapdoor: what you thought: consciousness is just awareness, the same for every school.
what it means: for Ramanuja, awareness always belongs to a self and shows an object, like a lamp's light.
what a scholar hears: the mahapurvapaksha and its answer in Sri Bhashya 1.1.1, with dharmabhuta-jnana, attributive consciousness, contracting and expanding.
recall: a warrior, and a daughter coming home
the year just walked and kept

sources.ref: Ramanuja, Sri Bhashya 1.1.1 (the great prior view and its answer: consciousness has a knower and an object; deep sleep; the lamp and its light)

notes: The Advaita view is summarized in one sentence (pure, objectless consciousness; the I superimposed, as a snake on a rope). An Advaita reader should confirm it is fair; the script says only that Advaita teachers answer in turn, without ranking.
The deep-sleep argument ('I slept well') and the lamp image are paraphrased from memory of the Sri Bhashya's opening section; confirm.
The term dharmabhuta-jnana belongs to the developed Vishishtadvaita vocabulary; confirm it fits Ramanuja himself, and check the Devanagari and stress.
